[**Classification of general-purpose AI models as general-purpose AI models with systemic risk**]
# **Classification of general-purpose AI models as general-purpose AI models with systemic risk**  
1. A general-purpose AI model shall be classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it meets any of the following conditions:  
- (a) it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks;  
- (b) based on a decision of the Commission, _ex officio_ or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those set out in point (a) having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII.  
2. A general-purpose AI model shall be presumed to have high impact capabilities pursuant to paragraph 1, point (a), when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training measured in floating point operations is greater than 10 25 .  
3. The Commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to amend the thresholds listed in paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Article, as well as to supplement benchmarks and indicators in light of evolving technological developments, such as algorithmic improvements or increased hardware efficiency, when necessary, for these thresholds to reflect the state of the art.

[**Procedure**]
# **Procedure**  
1. Where a general-purpose AI model meets the condition referred to in Article 51(1), point (a), the relevant provider shall notify the Commission without delay and in any event within two weeks after that requirement is met or it becomes known that it will be met. That notification shall include the information necessary to demonstrate that the relevant requirement has been met. If the Commission becomes aware of a general-purpose AI model presenting systemic risks of which it has not been notified, it may decide to designate it as a model with systemic risk.  
2. The provider of a general-purpose AI model that meets the condition referred to in Article 51(1), point (a), may present, with its notification, sufficiently substantiated arguments to demonstrate that, exceptionally, although it meets that requirement, the general-purpose AI model does not present, due to its specific characteristics, systemic risks and therefore should not be classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk.

# **Amendment to Regulation (EU) 2018/858**  
In Article 5 of Regulation (EU) 2018/858 the following paragraph is added:  
‘4. When adopting delegated acts pursuant to paragraph 3 concerning Artificial Intelligence systems which are safety components within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council (*), the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, of that Regulation shall be taken into account.  
- (*) Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) (OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/ 2024/1689/oj).’.

- (179) This Regulation should apply from 2 August 2026. However, taking into account the unacceptable risk associated with the use of AI in certain ways, the prohibitions as well as the general provisions of this Regulation should already apply from 2 February 2025. While the full effect of those prohibitions follows with the establishment of the governance and enforcement of this Regulation, anticipating the application of the prohibitions is important to take account of unacceptable risks and to have an effect on other procedures, such as in civil law. Moreover, the infrastructure related to the governance and the conformity assessment system should be operational before 2 August 2026, therefore the provisions on notified bodies and governance structure should apply from 2 August 2025. Given the rapid pace of technological advancements and adoption of general-purpose AI models, obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models should apply from 2 August 2025. Codes of practice should be ready by 2 May 2025 in view of enabling providers to demonstrate compliance on time. The AI Office should ensure that classification rules and procedures are up to date in light of technological developments. In addition, Member States should lay down and notify to the Commission the rules on penalties, including administrative fines, and ensure that they are properly and effectively implemented by the date of application of this Regulation. Therefore the provisions on penalties should apply from 2 August 2025.

After an expedited review of the comments by the Department, the Secretary decided that it was appropriate for the Privacy Rule to become effective on April 14, 2001, as scheduled (65 FR 12433). At the same time, the Secretary directed the Department immediately to begin the process of developing guidelines on how the Privacy Rule should be implemented and to clarify the impact of the Privacy Rule on health care activities. In addition, the Secretary charged the Department with proposing appropriate changes to the Privacy Rule during the next year to clarify the requirements and correct potential problems that could threaten access to, or quality of, health care. The comments received during the comment period, as well as other communications from the public and all sectors of the health care industry, including letters, testimony at public hearings, and meetings requested by these parties, have helped to inform the Department’s efforts to develop proposed modifications and guidance on the Privacy Rule.  
On July 6, 2001, the Department issued its first guidance to answer common questions and clarify certain of the Privacy Rule’s provisions. In the guidance, the Department also committed to proposing modifications to the Privacy Rule to address problems arising from unintended effects of the Privacy Rule on health care delivery and access. The guidance will soon be updated to reflect the modifications adopted in this final Rule. The revised guidance will be available on the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) Privacy Web site at _http://www.hhs.gov/ocr/ hipaa/._

[_A. Statutory Background_]
After a set of HIPAA Administrative Simplification standards is adopted by the Department, HIPAA provides HHS with authority to modify the standards as deemed appropriate, but not more frequently than once every 12 months. However, modifications are permitted during the first year after adoption of the standards if the changes are necessary to permit compliance with the standards. HIPAA also provides that compliance with modifications to standards or implementation specifications must be accomplished by a date designated by the Secretary, which may not be earlier than 180 days after the adoption of the modification.

The Protection of Personal Data Law No. 6698 came into force after its publication in the Official Gazette No. 29677 on 7 April 2016. Turkish Data Protection Authority was established under the same Law and is located in Ankara.  
Personal Data Protection Authority, which is a public legal entity and possesses administrative and financial autonomy, has been established to carry out duties conferred on it under the Law No. 6698. The Authority is composed of the Personal Data Protection Board and the Presidency.  
Personal Data Protection Board consists of nine members. Five members of the Board are elected by Grand National Assembly of Turkey, two members by the President of the Republic and two members by the Council of Ministers 1 . The selection and appointment process of the Board members was completed at the end of 2016 and the Board started its duty on January 12, 2017 after the members took the oath before the First Presidency Board of the Court of Cassation.  
The mission of the Authority is to ensure the protection of personal data and develop awareness in this respect in the public eye in line with the fundamental rights related with privacy and freedom stated in the Constitution as well as to establish an environment to enhance the capability of competition of the public and private organisations in the data-driven world. Our vision is to be a globally recognized competent authority which is influential in the protection of personal data and raising the public awareness in this regard.

audit_logs.input_question: How do the mandatory transparency disclosures under GDPR Article 13 and Article 14 differ in terms of timing and informing the data subject of the origin of the data?
audit_logs.generated_text:
Under GDPR Article 13 and Article 14, the mandatory transparency disclosures differ in terms of timing and the information regarding the origin of the data.

Article 13 requires the controller to provide the information referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 within a reasonable period after obtaining the personal data, but at the latest within one month. This includes informing the data subject about the origin of the personal data, unless the data subject already has the information, the provision of such information proves impossible or would involve a disproportionate effort, or other specific conditions apply as outlined in Article 13(5).

Article 14, on the other hand, mandates that the controller provide the information prior to further processing of personal data for a purpose other than that for which the personal data were obtained. This ensures that the data subject is informed before any additional processing takes place, and it also includes the origin of the personal data, subject to the same conditions as mentioned above.

In summary, Article 13 focuses on the initial collection and disclosure of personal data, while Article 14 addresses the need to inform the data subject before any further processing for a new purpose, with both requiring the disclosure of the data's origin.

transformed_question: Describe the escalation path under GDPR Articles 60 and 65 when a concerned supervisory authority raises a reasoned objection to a lead authority's draft decision, including the voting fallback if a two-thirds Board majority is not achieved.
ground_truth: Under Article 60(3)-(4), after the lead authority submits a draft decision, concerned authorities have four weeks to raise a relevant and reasoned objection; if the lead authority rejects or does not follow the objection, it submits the matter to the consistency mechanism under Article 63/65(1)(a) for a binding Board decision. Under Article 65(2)-(3), the Board adopts its binding decision by a two-thirds majority within one month (extendable by one month); if it fails to do so, it adopts the decision within two weeks after the second month by a simple majority, with the Chair casting the deciding vote in a tie.
generated_answer:
When a concerned supervisory authority raises a relevant and reasoned objection to a lead authority's draft decision, the following escalation path is outlined under GDPR Articles 60 and 65:

1. The lead supervisory authority must submit the revised draft decision to the concerned supervisory authorities for their opinion within two weeks.
2. If none of the concerned supervisory authorities object within the specified period, the lead authority and the concerned authorities are deemed to agree with the draft decision.
3. If an objection is raised, the lead supervisory authority and the concerned authorities must agree on the matter. If they fail to reach an agreement, the Board of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) will intervene.
4. The Board will issue a binding decision within one month, with a possible extension of one additional month for complex cases. This decision must be adopted by a two-thirds majority of the Board members.
5. If the Board cannot adopt a decision within the given periods, it will adopt a decision by a simple majority after the second month, with the Chair's vote deciding in case of a tie.

This ensures that the matter is resolved through structured and binding mechanisms to maintain consistency in the application of GDPR across different supervisory authorities.

original_question: Detail the multi-stage significant incident reporting timeline under NIS2 Directive Article 23(4), including the trust service provider derogation and the procedure if an incident is still ongoing after one month.
transformed_question: Detail the multi-stage significant incident reporting timeline under NIS2 Directive Article 23(4), including the trust service provider derogation and the procedure if an incident is still ongoing after one month.
ground_truth: Entities must submit: (1) an early warning within 24 hours of awareness indicating suspected unlawful/malicious cause or cross-border impact; (2) an incident notification within 72 hours with initial severity/impact assessment and indicators of compromise (by derogation, trust service providers must submit this notification within 24 hours); (3) an intermediate report upon CSIRT/authority request; and (4) a final report within one month after the incident notification detailing severity, root cause, mitigation, and cross-border impact. If the incident is still ongoing at one month, the entity submits a progress report then and a final report within one month of handling the incident.
generated_answer:
The multi-stage significant incident reporting timeline under NIS2 Directive Article 23(4) is as follows:

1. **Early Warning**: The entity concerned must submit an early warning without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident. This early warning should indicate whether the incident is suspected of being caused by unlawful or malicious acts and whether it is likely to have a cross-border impact.

2. **Incident Notification**: The entity must submit an incident notification without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident. This notification should update the information provided in the early warning and include an initial assessment of the incident, including its severity and impact, as well as indicators of compromise.

3. **Intermediate Report**: Upon request by a CSIRT or the competent authority, an intermediate report on relevant status updates should be provided.

4. **Final Report**: A final report should be submitted not later than one month after the submission of the incident notification. original_question: Compare the supervisory regimes and maximum administrative fine ceilings for essential entities versus important entities under NIS2 Directive Articles 32, 33, and 34.
transformed_question: Compare the supervisory regimes and maximum administrative fine ceilings for essential entities versus important entities under NIS2 Directive Articles 32, 33, and 34.
ground_truth: Essential entities (Article 32) face proactive/ex ante and ex post supervision (on-site/off-site random checks, regular/targeted/ad hoc audits, monitoring officers, and temporary certification suspension or CEO managerial bans if orders fail) and fines of a maximum of at least EUR 10,000,000 or 2% of worldwide annual turnover (Article 34(4)). Important entities (Article 33) are subject to ex post supervision triggered by evidence, indication, or information of non-compliance (without certification suspension or managerial bans) and fines of a maximum of at least EUR 7,000,000 or 1.4% of worldwide annual turnover (Article 34(5)).
generated_answer:
Under the NIS2 Directive Articles 32, 33, and 34, the supervisory and enforcement regimes for essential and important entities differ as follows:

### Supervisory Regimes:
- **Essential Entities:**
  - Subject to a comprehensive _ex ante_ and _ex post_ supervisory regime.
  - Require systematic documentation of compliance with cybersecurity risk-management measures.
  - Subject to on-site inspections, off-site supervision, regular and targeted security audits, ad hoc audits, and security scans.
  
- **Important Entities:**
  - Subject to a light, _ex post_ only, supervisory regime.
  - Not required to systematically document compliance with cybersecurity risk-management measures.
  - Subject to _ex post_ supervision triggered by evidence, indication, or information brought to the attention of the competent authorities.

### Maximum Administrative Fine Ceilings:
- **Essential Entities:**
  - Maximum administrative fines of at least EUR 10,000,000 or 2% of the total worldwide annual turnover in the preceding financial year of the undertaking to which the essential entity belongs, whichever is higher.
  
- **Important Entities:**
  - Maximum administrative fines of at least EUR 7,000,000 or 1.4% of the total worldwide annual turnover in the preceding financial year of the undertaking to which the important entity belongs, whichever is higher.
contexts: - (122) In order to strengthen the supervisory powers and measures that help ensure effective compliance, this Directive should provide for a minimum list of supervisory measures and means through which the competent authorities can supervise essential and important entities. In addition, this Directive should establish a differentiation of supervisory regime between essential and important entities with a view to ensuring a fair balance of obligations on those entities and on the competent authorities. Therefore, essential entities should be subject to a comprehensive _ex ante_ and _ex post_ supervisory regime, while important entities should be subject to a light, _ex post_ only, supervisory regime. Important entities should therefore not be required to systematically document compliance with cybersecurity risk-management measures, while the competent authorities should implement a reactive _ex post_ approach to supervision and, hence, not have a general obligation to supervise those entities. The _ex post_ supervision of important entities may be triggered by evidence, indication or information brought to the attention of the competent authorities considered by those authorities to suggest potential infringements of this Directive. For example, such evidence, indication or information could be of the type provided to the competent authorities by other authorities, entities, citizens, media or other sources or publicly available information, or could emerge from other activities conducted by the competent authorities in the fulfilment of their tasks.

ground_truth: The 2002 Final Rule eliminated the December 2000 mandatory prior consent requirement for direct treatment providers, amending § 164.506 to permit covered entities to use or disclose PHI for treatment, payment, and health care operations without prior consent while making consent optional (§ 164.506(b)). To preserve patient awareness, § 164.520(c)(2)(ii) was added requiring direct treatment providers—except in emergency treatment situations—to make a good faith effort to obtain written acknowledgment of receipt of the Notice of Privacy Practices and to document their good faith efforts and reasons if acknowledgment is not obtained.

The 2002 HIPAA Privacy Rule Final Rule modified § 164.506 by eliminating the requirement for covered health care providers to obtain an individual’s consent to use or disclose protected health information for treatment, payment, and health care operations, except in certain circumstances. This change was made to streamline the process and ensure that core health care activities could continue without unnecessary barriers.

To address the loss of the consent requirement, the rule added a new documentation duty under § 164.520(c)(2), which requires covered health care providers with a direct treatment relationship to make a good faith effort to obtain the individual’s acknowledgment of receipt of the notice of privacy practices provided at the first service delivery. This acknowledgment can be as simple as retaining a copy of the notice initialed by the individual. If the provider’s good faith effort fails, documentation of the attempt is sufficient.

However, it violates the Privacy Rule if it results from a failure to apply reasonable safeguards or the minimum necessary standard, where required.

Specifically, § 164.530(c) requires covered entities to implement appropriate administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to reasonably safeguard protected health information. The minimum necessary standard, as required by § 164.502(b) and 164.514(d), mandates that covered entities develop and implement policies and procedures to reasonably minimize the amount of protected health information used, disclosed, and requested. These policies and procedures must identify the persons or classes of persons within the covered entity who need access to the information to carry out their job duties, the categories or types of protected health information needed, and the conditions appropriate to such access. Non-routine requests for, and disclosures of, protected health information must be reviewed individually.

Under Article 9, transferring personal data abroad without explicit consent to a country without adequate protection requires: (1) the existence of a condition in Article 5(2) or Article 6(3); (2) a written commitment of adequate protection by the data controllers in Turkey and in the foreign country; and (3) authorisation of the Board.

original_question: Compare the core content required in a Data Protection Impact Assessment under GDPR Article 35(7) versus a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment under EU AI Act Article 27(1), and explain how AI Act Article 26(9) connects them.
transformed_question: Compare the core content required in a Data Protection Impact Assessment under GDPR Article 35(7) versus a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment under EU AI Act Article 27(1), and explain how AI Act Article 26(9) connects them.
ground_truth: GDPR Article 35(7) requires a systematic description of processing/purposes, necessity and proportionality assessment, assessment of risks to data subjects' rights and freedoms, and envisaged safeguards/security measures. EU AI Act Article 27(1) requires covered deployers of high-risk AI systems to assess deployment processes, time period/frequency of use, affected persons/groups, specific risks of harm (using Article 13 provider info), human oversight implementation, and risk-materialization governance/complaint measures. Under AI Act Article 26(9), deployers of high-risk AI systems must use the transparency information provided under AI Act Article 13 to comply with their GDPR Article 35 DPIA obligations.
generated_answer:
The core content required in a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR Article 35(7) and a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) under the EU AI Act Article 27(1) share some similarities but also have distinct focuses.

### Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR Article 35(7):
- **Nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement and its consequences**: Evaluating the nature, severity, and duration of potential data breaches or misuse.
- **Degree of responsibility of the data controller or processor**: Assessing the responsibility of the entity handling the data.
- **Action taken to mitigate damage**: Identifying measures taken to prevent or mitigate harm.
- **Cooperation with the European Data Protection Supervisor**: Ensuring collaboration with supervisory authorities.
- **Similar previous infringements**: Considering any past incidents.
- **Manner of becoming aware of the infringement**: Determining how the infringement was discovered.

### Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) under EU AI Act Article 27(1):
- **Description of the deployer’s processes**: Detailing how the AI system will be integrated into existing operations.
- **Period and frequency of use**: Specifying the timeline and frequency of AI system deployment.
- **Categories of affected individuals**: Identifying the groups that may be impacted.
- **Specific risks of harm**: Assessing potential harms to individuals.
- **Human oversight measures**: Describing the oversight mechanisms in place.
- **Measures to address risks**: Outlining steps to mitigate identified risks.

### Connection via AI Act Article 26(9):
AI Act Article 26(9) states that if any of the obligations under the AI Act are already met through a data protection impact assessment conducted under Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the fundamental rights impact assessment should complement that assessment. This means that while a DPIA focuses primarily on data protection, an FRIA must consider broader fundamental rights implications. The AI Act Article 26(9) ensures that the FRIA builds upon the existing DPIA, integrating additional fundamental rights considerations to ensure a comprehensive assessment of the AI system's impact.

audit_logs.generated_text:
The core content required in a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR Article 35(7) and a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) under the EU AI Act Article 27(1) share some similarities but also have distinct focuses.

### Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR Article 35(7):
- **Nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement and its consequences**: Evaluating the nature, severity, and duration of potential data breaches or misuse.
- **Degree of responsibility of the data controller or processor**: Assessing the responsibility of the entity handling the data.
- **Action taken to mitigate damage**: Identifying measures taken to prevent or mitigate harm.
- **Cooperation with the European Data Protection Supervisor**: Ensuring collaboration with supervisory authorities.
- **Similar previous infringements**: Considering any past incidents.
- **Manner of becoming aware of the infringement**: Determining how the infringement was discovered.

### Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) under EU AI Act Article 27(1):
- **Description of the deployer’s processes**: Detailing how the AI system will be integrated into existing operations.
- **Period and frequency of use**: Specifying the timeline and frequency of AI system deployment.
- **Categories of affected individuals**: Identifying the groups that may be impacted.
- **Specific risks of harm**: Assessing potential harms to individuals.
- **Human oversight measures**: Describing the oversight mechanisms in place.
- **Measures to address risks**: Outlining steps to mitigate identified risks.

### Connection via AI Act Article 26(9):
AI Act Article 26(9) states that if any of the obligations under the AI Act are already met through a data protection impact assessment conducted under Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the fundamental rights impact assessment should complement that assessment. This means that while a DPIA focuses primarily on data protection, an FRIA must consider broader fundamental rights implications. The AI Act Article 26(9) ensures that the FRIA builds upon the existing DPIA, integrating additional fundamental rights considerations to ensure a comprehensive assessment of the AI system's impact.

ground_truth: GDPR Article 33(1) requires controllers to notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness (with phased updates allowed under Article 33(4) if full info is unavailable). NIS2 Article 23(4) establishes a stricter multi-stage timeline: an early warning within 24 hours of awareness, a formal incident notification within 72 hours (or 24 hours for trust service providers), optional intermediate reports on request, and a comprehensive final report within one month after the incident notification (or a progress report if ongoing).

Under EU GDPR Article 33, the controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach, unless the controller can demonstrate that the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

In contrast, the EU NIS2 Directive Article 23(4) introduces additional stages before and after the 72-hour mark for significant incidents:

1. **Early Warning**: Entities must submit an early warning without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident. This early warning should include whether the incident is suspected of being caused by unlawful or malicious acts and whether it could have a cross-border impact.

2. **Incident Notification**: Following the early warning, entities must submit an incident notification without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident. This notification should update the information provided in the early warning and include an initial assessment of the incident, its severity and impact, and indicators of compromise, if available.

3. **Intermediate Report**: Upon request by the CSIRT or competent authority, entities must provide an intermediate report on relevant status updates.

4. **Final Report**: Entities must submit a final report not later than one month after the incident notification, detailing the incident, the type of threat or root cause, applied and ongoing mitigation measures, and the cross-border impact, if applicable.

Under NIS2 Article 35(2), if a GDPR supervisory authority imposes an administrative fine under GDPR Article 58(2)(i) for the same conduct, the NIS2 competent authority is barred from imposing a NIS2 Article 34 monetary fine, though non-monetary NIS2 enforcement measures remain permitted.

ground_truth: GDPR Article 9(1) broadly prohibits processing health data unless an Article 9(2) exception applies—such as explicit consent (9(2)(a)) or preventive/occupational medicine, medical diagnosis, and health/social care management by professionals subject to secrecy (9(2)(h)). ground_truth: EU AI Act Article 73 sets severity-tiered deadlines to market surveillance authorities: up to 15 days generally (Art 73(2)), up to 10 days in the event of a person's death (Art 73(4)), and up to 2 days for widespread infringements or critical-infrastructure serious incidents under Article 3(49)(b) (Art 73(3)). By contrast, NIS2 Article 23(4) mandates phased reporting to CSIRTs/competent authorities: a 24-hour early warning, a 72-hour incident notification (24 hours for trust service providers), optional intermediate updates, and a final report within one month.

transformed_question: Compare the right to lodge a complaint with a regulatory authority under EU AI Act Article 85 versus Turkish KVKK Law No. 6698 Articles 13 and 14, specifically regarding who may complain and whether a prior application to the operator/controller is mandatory.
ground_truth: Under EU AI Act Article 85, any natural or legal person having grounds to consider an infringement occurred may submit a complaint directly to the relevant market surveillance authority without needing to exhaust a prior request to the AI operator. Under Turkish KVKK Articles 13 and 14, only natural persons (data subjects) are protected, and the data subject cannot contact the Personal Data Protection Board before first exhausting the mandatory remedy of applying to the data controller (and only then complaining within 30 days of learning the response or 60 days from application).
generated_answer:
Under the EU AI Act Article 85, every data subject has the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority if they consider that the processing of personal data relating to them infringes the Regulation. There is no requirement for the data subject to exhaust remedies with the controller before lodging a complaint with the supervisory authority.

In contrast, according to Turkish KVKK Law No. 6698 Articles 13 and 14, if a data subject's request to the controller is refused, found insufficient, or not answered within 30 days, the data subject may lodge a complaint with the Board. However, a data subject whose request has been refused, either implicitly or explicitly, may both lodge a complaint with the Board and resort directly to judicial or administrative jurisdiction without exhausting the remedy with the controller first. 

Therefore, while both frameworks allow direct complaints to the supervisory authority, the EU AI Act does not require prior application to the controller, whereas the Turkish KVKK Law requires the data subject to first address the controller before complaining to the Board.

[_A. Summary of Costs and Benefits in the December 2000 Regulatory Impact Statement_]
### _A. Summary of Costs and Benefits in the December 2000 Regulatory Impact Statement_  
The Privacy Rule was estimated to produce net costs of $17.6 billion, with net present value costs of $11.8 billion (2003 dollars) over ten years (2003– 2012). The Department estimates the modifications in this proposal would lower the net cost of the Privacy Rule by approximately $100 million over ten years.  
Measuring both the economic costs and benefits of health information privacy was recognized as a difficult task. The paucity of data and incomplete information on current industry privacy and information system practices made cost estimation a challenge. Benefits were difficult to measure because they are, for the most part, inherently intangible. Therefore, the regulatory impact analysis in the Privacy Rule focused on the key policy  
areas addressed by the privacy standards, some of which are affected by the modifications adopted in this rulemaking.  
_B. Proposed Modifications To Prevent Barriers to Access to or Quality of Health Care_  
The modifications adopted in this rulemaking are intended to address the possible adverse effects of the final privacy standards on an individual’s access to, or the quality of, health care. The modifications touch on five of the key policy areas addressed by the final regulatory impact analysis, including consent, research, marketing, notice, and business associates.

[5. Research]
### 5. Research  
In the final impact analysis of the December 2000 Privacy Rule, the Department estimated the total cost of the provisions requiring documentation of an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or Privacy Board waiver of individual authorization for the use or disclosure of protected health information for a research purpose as $40 million for the first year and $585 million for the tenyear period. The costs were estimated based on the time that an IRB or Privacy Board would need to consider a request for a waiver under the criteria provided in the Privacy Rule. _See_ 65 FR 82770– 82771 (December 28, 2000).  
The modifications simplify and reduce the number of criteria required for an IRB or Privacy Board to approve a waiver of authorization to better conform to the Common Rule’s waiver criteria for informed consent to participate in the research study. The Department estimates that the net effect of these modifications is to reduce the time necessary to assemble the waivers and for an IRB or Privacy Board to consider and act on waiver requests by one quarter. The Department estimates these simplifications would reduce the expected costs first year costs by $10 million and the ten year costs by $146 million, relative to the December 2000 Privacy Rule. Although the Department requested information to better assess this cost savings, the public comment period failed to produce any sound data. Therefore, the Department’s estimates have not changed.

[**IV. Final Regulatory Impact Analysis**]
The December 2000 preamble to the Privacy Rule included a regulatory impact analysis (RIA), which estimated the cost of the Privacy Rule at $17.6 billion over ten years. 65 FR 82462, 82758. The modifications to the Privacy Rule adopted by this rulemaking are a result of comment by the industry and the public at large identifying a number of unintended consequences of the Privacy Rule that could adversely affect access to, or the quality of, health care delivery. These modifications should facilitate implementation and compliance with the Privacy Rule, and lower the costs and burdens associated with the Privacy Rule while maintaining  
the confidentiality of protected health information. The Department estimates the impact of the modifications adopted in this rulemaking will be a net reduction of costs associated with the Privacy Rule of at least $100 million over ten years.

[**II. Overview of the March 2002 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM)**]
### **II. Overview of the March 2002 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM)**  
As described above, through public comments, testimony at public hearings, meetings at the request of industry and other stakeholders, as well as other communications, the Department learned of a number of concerns about the potential unintended effects certain provisions would have on health care quality and access. On March 27, 2002, in response to these concerns, and pursuant to HIPAA’s provisions for modifications to the standards, the Department proposed modifications to the Privacy Rule (67 FR 14776).  
The Department proposed to modify the following areas or provisions of the Privacy Rule: consent; uses and disclosures for treatment, payment, and health care operations; notice of privacy practices; minimum necessary uses and disclosures, and oral communications; business associates; uses and disclosures for marketing; parents as the personal representatives of unemancipated minors; uses and disclosures for research purposes; uses and disclosures for which authorizations are required; and deidentification. In addition to these key areas, the proposal included changes to other provisions where necessary to clarify the Privacy Rule. The Department also included in the proposed Rule a list of technical corrections intended as editorial or typographical corrections to the Privacy Rule.
